newsitem.title: GERMANY: VW H1 1997 profits seen racing ahead.
newsitem.headline: VW H1 1997 profits seen racing ahead.

text.p: German carmaker Volkswagen AG will pick up where it left off last year when it publishes first-half results for 1997 early next week that are expected to show another solid jump in profits, analysts said.

Car industry analysts expect VW to report group net profit climbed to around 500 million marks ($271.3 million) during the first six months of the year from 282 million marks during the first half of 1996. Sales are forecast to rise to about 56 billion marks from 50 billion.
VW profits, after years well below other carmakers, are now speeding ahead, reflecting strict cost-cutting efforts, popular new cars and like all German car companies -- the strong dollar.
"VW will continue to go up in financial terms," said Peter Schmidt, analyst at British research group Auto Industry Data. "They are really starting to make money."
Volkswagen is scheduled to publish first-half results on Tuesday, August 19.
In February, Volkswagen announced 1996 group net profit doubled to 678 million marks on the back of a 14 percent increase in sales to 100.1 billion marks.

Analysts said the continued profit and sales growth comes as a victory for VW which is facing difficulty in its home market and a change-over of its mainstay Golf model that has hurt demand for one of Europe's top selling cars.
Popular models such as the Passat and Polo as well as cars made by its Audi luxury car unit, are keeping sales climbing steadily, analysts said.

"The success of recent model introductions is supporting the VW group's sales ahead of the change-over of the crucial VW Golf," wrote Sabine Bluemel, analyst at IMI Sigeco in a commentary ahead of the results.
Volkswagen has already flagged sales growth, saying in July first-half group turnover rose 9.8 percent to 2.194 million units but did not provide a mark value.
Sales have also come in the right places for VW with demand climbing for the Passat and Audi -- models with a higher profit margin than other models such as the Polo.
Audi, which reported first-half figures earlier this month, saw pre-tax profit increase 20.9 percent to 489 million marks. Sales climbed 13.7 percent to 10.60 billion marks.
Analysts said VW's non-German units also made a solid contribution to group results.

Sales at its Czech unit Skoda Automobilova a.s., for example, climbed 27.2 percent in the first half of the year to 161,886 cars and the company has set a growth target of 30 percent, or 340,000 cars to be produced and sold for the whole of 1997.
"Skoda has made tremendous improvement in its image," Schmidt said. "Skoda is one of the biggest success stories in the European car industry."
Seat said in March it made a net profit of 5.34 billion pesetas in 1996, its first time in the black for three years.
The performance was boosted by a series of exceptional items, but the company said it hopes to make a profit in 1997 without any external aid. ($ = 1.842 German Marks)
